pr_title: Return 400 bad request when IOException is thrown when ready form.
pr_body:
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/47525

Currently if someone uploads a file and that file exceeds what is specified in `KestrelServerOptions` an `IOException` will be thrown when we attempt to read from the HTTP stream. However, the request delegate that we produce silently swallows this and results in the HTTP response being 200 which is obviously problematic.

This change tweaks the logic such that if an `IOException` is raised, it is returned as a 400 bad request. This PR addresses the issue linked above, but we probably need to satisfy ourselves that this is the correct response. Some questions:

Is 400 the right response here? Would it make more sense to throw a more specific exception out of Kestrel (and other servers) and return a 413?

Somewhat related, when FormOptions is specified, we can specify a maximum body size for the form, when we do that we get a 400 error - should this be a 413 instead also?

```
Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.BadHttpRequestException: Failed to read parameter "IFormFile file" from the request body as form.
 ---> System.IO.InvalidDataException: Multipart body length limit 50 exceeded.
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.WebUtilities.MultipartReaderStream.UpdatePosition(Int32 read) in C:\Code\dotnet\aspnetcore\src\Http\WebUtilities\src\MultipartReaderStream.cs:line 150
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.WebUtilities.MultipartReaderStream.ReadAsync(Memory`1 buffer, CancellationToken cancellationToken) in C:\Code\dotnet\aspnetcore\src\Http\WebUtilities\src\MultipartReaderStream.cs:line 238
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.WebUtilities.FileBufferingReadStream.ReadAsync(Memory`1 buffer, CancellationToken cancellationToken) in C:\Code\dotnet\aspnetcore\src\Http\WebUtilities\src\FileBufferingReadStream.cs:line 344
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.WebUtilities.StreamHelperExtensions.DrainAsync(Stream stream, ArrayPool`1 bytePool, Nullable`1 limit, CancellationToken cancellationToken) in C:\Code\dotnet\aspnetcore\src\Http\WebUtilities\src\StreamHelperExtensions.cs:line 62
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Features.FormFeature.InnerReadFormAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken) in C:\Code\dotnet\aspnetcore\src\Http\Http\src\Features\FormFeature.cs:line 206
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.RequestDelegateFactory.<HandleRequestBodyAndCompileRequestDelegateForForm>g__TryReadFormAsync|96_0(HttpContext httpContext, String parameterTypeName, String parameterName, Boolean throwOnBadRequest) in C:\Code\dotnet\aspnetcore\src\Http\Http.Extensions\src\RequestDelegateFactory.cs:line 1420
   --- End of inner exception stack trace ---
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.RequestDelegateFactory.Log.InvalidFormRequestBody(HttpContext httpContext, String parameterTypeName, String parameterName, Exception exception, Boolean shouldThrow) in C:\Code\dotnet\aspnetcore\src\Http\Http.Extensions\src\RequestDelegateFactory.cs:line 2468
```
pr_comments:
> Is 400 the right response here? Would it make more sense to throw a more specific exception out of Kestrel (and other servers) and return a 413?

The actual exception is a BadHttpRequestException : IOException right? That includes a status code you can set on the response.

For other IOExceptions, 400 seems fine.

> Somewhat related, when FormOptions is specified, we can specify a maximum body size for the form, when we do that we get a 400 error - should this be a 413 instead also?

The InvalidDataException could be thrown for several reasons, not just size issues. If we wanted to communicate more information we'd have to put it into the IDE's data collection, or make a new derived exception.

> The actual exception is a BadHttpRequestException : IOException right? That includes a status code you can set on the response.

This particular codepath doesn't use a `BadHttpRequestException` since it handles `IOExceptions` emitted during exception process which abort request handling instead of indicating that the response itself that was read isn't valid.

@mitchdenny's recommendation here:

>  Would it make more sense to throw a more specific exception out of Kestrel (and other servers) and return a 413?

would allow us to return a 4xx style error for the specific case where the IOException was triggered because it didn't match the constraints set in the Kestrel config.

As to the general question of whether we should throw more specific exceptions from the underlying APIs (Kestrel/form-processing) and return 413s, I worry that the cost of additional APIs/logic in the underlying layer might not be worth the benefit.

@captainsafia @Tratcher updated PR to handle BadHttpRequestException specifically AND use the status code stored on the exception. For now, I'm filtering the exception for just the 413 scenarios as I'd like to be able to backport this change if possible since I think this bug represents a possible data loss scenario for folks - hence being as conservative as possible.

issue_context.title: [Minimal API] Incorrect response when request body is too large
issue_context.body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

I'm using .NET 7.0.4 and I'm trying to change the `MaxRequestBodySize` property in Kestrel:

    var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
    
    builder.WebHost.ConfigureKestrel(options =>
    {
        options.Limits.MaxRequestBodySize = 1024;
    });

With this setting, if I use a classic Controller like this:

    [ApiController]
    [Route("api/[controller]")]
    [Produces(MediaTypeNames.Application.Json)]
    public class UploadController : ControllerBase
    {
        [HttpPost("with_controller")]
        public IActionResult Upload(IFormFile file) => NoContent();
    }

When I try to upload a file larger that 1024 bytes, I obtain the following error:

    {
      "type": "https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7231#section-6.5.1",
      "title": "One or more validation errors occurred.",
      "status": 400,
      "traceId": "00-5392ad98781087812b2bba29374a2a21-ce7ed0cde6248257-00",
      "errors": {
        "": [
          "Failed to read the request form. Request body too large. The max request body size is 1024 bytes."
        ]
      }
    }

However, if I use a Minimal API endpoint:

`app.MapPost("api/upload/with_minimalapi", (IFormFile file) => TypedResults.NoContent());`

And try to upload the same file that excedees 1024 bytes, I obtain a 200 OK response:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3522534/229283040-9cc9950f-a280-4014-87f7-557429378a23.png)

### Expected Behavior

The Minimal API endpoint should return a 400 Bad Request response, like the Controller.

### Steps To Reproduce

Minimal repro: https://github.com/marcominerva/UploadMaxSizeIssue

### Exceptions (if any)

_No response_

### .NET Version

7.0.202

### Anything else?

_No response_
comments:
Thanks for reporting this @marcominerva. I dug into this a bit today to try and figure out what was going on here. There are two sets of limits that come into play when we talk about minimal APIs. The first one that you've highlighted is ```MaxRequestBodySize``` which is set via ```KestrelServerOptions```.

When minimal APIs goes to bind the ```IFormFile``` parameter it makes a request to ```HttpContext.Request.ReadFormAsync(...)``` which ultimately checks the content length against the max body here:

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/0b10e1349063b1b5b39dd0435509abb52cc81d90/src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/Internal/Http2/Http2MessageBody.cs#L30

That throws and is caught here:

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/0b10e1349063b1b5b39dd0435509abb52cc81d90/src/Http/Http.Extensions/src/RequestDelegateFactory.cs#L1421

I haven't had a closer look at why it doesn't result in a BadRequest yet, but the problem is in there somewhere. I also had a look at possible work arounds for this issue.

For the time being you could add something like this:

```csharp
builder.Services.Configure<FormOptions>(fo =>
{
    fo.MultipartBodyLengthLimit = 1024; // 1KB
});
```

Actually here is where we drop the ball:

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/0b10e1349063b1b5b39dd0435509abb52cc81d90/src/Http/Http.Extensions/src/RequestDelegateFactory.cs#LL1370C25-L1370C25

You can see if reading from the form isn't successful we just return which is what causes the 200 response.
Thank you for the explanation! So, can we consider this behavior a bug?

I think returning a 200 when an error actually occurred is definitely an issue and probably a bug. But I'm I need to find out a bit more about why it is like this. There might be something that I'm not across.

@houseofcat as mentioned on the issue you opened, I closed it as a dupe of this issue (lets try and keep the conversation in one place). In terms of fixing the issue I think that there is a case for two approaches with errors. One is a 500, and the other is 400.

Generally speaking, for parameter binding errors we return a 400. But this one is a little bit more interesting because we are actually failing because of a max request size limit which is independent of parameter binding.

There is also the behavior of what happens when we exceed size limits placed on `FormOptions` - we probably want to be consistent with the error that is raised there.

The case for 400 is that its consistent with other parameter binding errors.
The case for 500 is that the error has more to do with the overall HTTP request size.
Does the IOException provide the information internally to be distinct for you? I.e. in Exception Code/HResult/Data. Obviously we don't want to parse the string for "an exception phrase".

review_comments:
IOException should still set a non-default status code like 400 if it's not going to be propagated, otherwise there are probably similar ways to hit the same issue.

E.g. https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/7d0c27344d193cb6ad263732d1fef6d3e0fd1f71/src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/KestrelBadHttpRequestException.cs#L70-L71
Discussed offline w/Safia. You should be able to add another catch block here for BadHttpRequestException and use the StatusCode it provides.
Thought this might be where we land. I'll make the change.
